entities.summary:
Fernando Pérez Calvillo (b. c. 1350, Tarazona, Kingdom of Aragon – d. 1404-07-30, Avignon, Papal States) was a prominent Aragonese cleric whose career was inextricably linked to the tumultuous Western Schism (1378-1417). Elevated to Bishop of Tarazona in 1391 and later Cardinal-Priest of Santa Prisca by Antipope Benedict XIII in 1397, Calvillo served as a steadfast pillar of the Avignon obedience, wielding significant ecclesiastical and diplomatic influence during a period of profound fragmentation within the Catholic Church. His unwavering loyalty to Benedict XIII, despite growing calls for unity and the withdrawal of support from various European monarchs, underscored the deep ideological and political divisions that defined late medieval Christendom.

Calvillo's most notable contributions involved his active participation in the complex diplomatic maneuvers surrounding the schism. As a cardinal, he was a key advisor to Benedict XIII, defending the legitimacy of the Avignon line against the Roman pontiffs. He was instrumental in managing the curia at Avignon, particularly during the protracted siege of the papal palace by French forces between 1398 and 1403, a period that saw Benedict XIII effectively imprisoned. Calvillo's administrative acumen and political astuteness were crucial in maintaining the operations and limited authority of the Avignon papacy during its most challenging years, even as its sphere of influence dramatically shrank.

entities.summary:
Fernando Pérez Calvillo (1350, Tarazona – 30 July 1404) was a pivotal Aragonese ecclesiastic and diplomat whose career was inextricably linked to the tumultuous Western Schism (1378–1417). As Bishop of Tarazona and later a cardinal, he emerged as one of the most trusted and influential advisors to Antipope Benedict XIII, often referred to as 'Papa Luna'. His actions significantly shaped the political and religious landscape of the Crown of Aragon and beyond, as he tirelessly worked to legitimize and defend the Avignon papacy amidst a fractured Christendom, demonstrating the profound entanglement of secular power with spiritual authority during the late Medieval period.

Born in Tarazona, Pérez Calvillo rose through the ecclesiastical ranks, becoming Bishop of his native city in 1391. His diplomatic acumen quickly became apparent, leading to his elevation as cardinal by Benedict XIII in 1397, a period when the schism was at its most intractable. He undertook numerous missions on behalf of Benedict XIII, traveling across Europe to secure allegiance from monarchs and to counter the influence of the Roman pontiffs. Notably, he played a crucial role in the negotiations at the Council of Perpignan (1408) and was instrumental in shaping Benedict XIII's strategy to maintain his claim to the papacy, even as major powers like France began to withdraw their obedience from Avignon. His efforts included advocating for Benedict XIII's theological justifications and political legitimacy, often against formidable opposition from both secular and ecclesiastical authorities who sought to end the schism through alternative means.
